title: Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP): Core
summary: Defines the core of the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP), a way of streaming XML elements between two network endpoints in close to real time. It is a general framework, but is mainly used to build instant messaging and presence systems. It was replaced by RFC 6120.

plainLanguage.summary: XMPP is a way to keep a conversation open over the network and pass small pieces of structured information back and forth on it. This document defines the core: how each endpoint is addressed, how the two sides set up a protected channel and prove who they are, and the three kinds of message that travel on it. It is a general framework, but it is used mostly for instant messaging and presence.

subtitle: A framework for streaming XML between two endpoints, built mainly for instant messaging and presence.

tldr.problem: Applications built on the Jabber protocols worked, but the syntax and semantics had never been written down as an Internet standard, so implementations from different projects could not be relied on to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: XMPP defines an XML stream carried over TCP, three kinds of stanza sent inside it, an addressing scheme built on domain, node and resource names, and a negotiation sequence of TLS, SASL and resource binding before any stanza is sent.
tldr.outcome: The RFC turns a set of community conventions into a standard protocol that other applications can build on. RFC 3920 was obsoleted by RFC 6120.

today: RFC 3920 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 6120. It was updated by RFC 6122.

sections.title: The Generalized Architecture
sections.content:
XMPP is an open XML protocol for near-real-time messaging, presence and request-response services. The basic syntax and semantics were developed originally within the Jabber open-source community, mainly in 1999, and in 2002 the XMPP Working Group was chartered with developing an adaptation of the Jabber protocol suitable as an IETF instant messaging and presence technology. The extensions required for the functionality defined in RFC 2779 are specified separately in the XMPP Instant Messaging and Presence document.

Although XMPP is not tied to any specific network architecture, it has usually been implemented with a client-server architecture, in which a client accesses a server over a TCP connection and servers communicate with each other over TCP connections. A server acts as an intelligent abstraction layer. Its primary responsibilities are to manage connections from or sessions for other entities, in the form of XML streams to and from authorized clients, servers and other entities, and to route appropriately addressed XML stanzas among such entities over those streams. Most compliant servers also take responsibility for storing data used by clients, such as contact lists, and in that case the XML data is processed by the server on the client's behalf rather than routed to another entity.

Most clients connect directly to a server over TCP. Multiple resources, such as devices or locations, may connect simultaneously to a server on behalf of each authorized client, with each resource differentiated by the resource identifier of its address, such as node@domain/home against node@domain/work. The recommended port for connections between a client and a server is 5222.

A gateway is a special-purpose server-side service whose primary function is to translate XMPP into the protocol used by a foreign messaging system, and to translate the return data back into XMPP. The RFC names gateways to email, Internet Relay Chat, SIMPLE, Short Message Service and legacy instant messaging services such as AIM, ICQ, MSN Messenger and Yahoo! Instant Messenger, and notes that the communications between gateways and servers, and between gateways and the foreign system, are not defined in this document.

Because each server is identified by a network address, and because server-to-server communication is a straightforward extension of the client-to-server protocol, the system in practice consists of a network of servers that inter-communicate, so that a user at one domain can exchange messages with a user at another. Communications between any two servers are OPTIONAL, and if enabled should occur over XML streams bound to TCP connections. The recommended port for connections between servers is 5269.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients talk to servers, and servers talk to each other, so the whole network is a set of connected servers. A server does two jobs: it keeps the open connections and routes each piece of information to the right place. A gateway sits on the edge and translates between XMPP and some other messaging system, such as email or IRC.

sections.title: Addressing with JIDs
sections.content:
An entity is anything that can be considered a network endpoint and that can communicate using XMPP. All such entities are uniquely addressable in a form consistent with RFC 2396. For historical reasons, the address of an XMPP entity is called a Jabber Identifier, or JID. A valid JID contains a set of ordered elements formed of a domain identifier, a node identifier and a resource identifier.

The syntax is given in Augmented Backus-Naur Form as jid = [ node "@" ] domain [ "/" resource ], where the domain is either a fully qualified domain name or an address literal, which may be an IPv4 or IPv6 address. The allowable character sequences for the node rule are defined by the Nodeprep profile of stringprep and for the resource rule by the Resourceprep profile.

The most common use of the structure is to identify an instant messaging user, the server to which the user connects, and the user's connected resource, in the form user@host/resource. Other node types are possible: a chat room offered by a multi-user chat service could be addressed as room@service, and a specific occupant of such a room as room@service/nick. Many other JID types are possible, such as domain/resource for a server-side script or service.

Each allowable portion of a JID, whether node, domain or resource identifier, MUST NOT be more than 1023 bytes in length, which gives a maximum total size of 3071 bytes including the '@' and '/' separators. The domain identifier is the primary identifier and the only REQUIRED element of a JID, since a bare domain identifier is a valid JID. It usually represents the network gateway or primary server to which other entities connect, though the entity it refers to is not always a server and may be a service addressed as a subdomain of a server, such as a multi-user chat service, a user directory or a gateway to a foreign messaging system.
sections.plainLanguage: Every participant has an address with up to three parts: a name, the domain that owns it, and an optional resource that says which of the user's devices or sessions this is. The domain alone is a valid address, and each part has a length limit, so a whole address cannot exceed 3071 bytes.

sections.title: XML Streams
sections.content:
Two fundamental concepts make possible the rapid, asynchronous exchange of relatively small payloads of structured information between presence-aware entities: XML streams and XML stanzas. An XML stream is a container for the exchange of XML elements between any two entities over a network. Its start is denoted by an opening <stream> tag with appropriate attributes and namespace declarations, and its end by the matching closing tag. During the life of the stream the initiating entity can send an unbounded number of XML elements over it, either elements used to negotiate the stream, such as those used to negotiate TLS or SASL, or XML stanzas. The initial stream is negotiated from the initiating entity to the receiving entity and enables unidirectional communication; to enable information exchange in the other direction, the receiving entity MUST negotiate a stream in the opposite direction, the response stream.

An XML stanza is a discrete semantic unit of structured information sent from one entity to another over an XML stream. A stanza exists at the direct child level of the root <stream/> element, and the start of any stanza is denoted by the element start tag at depth one of the XML stream, and its end by the corresponding close tag at depth one. A stanza may contain child elements as necessary to convey the desired information. An element sent for the purpose of TLS negotiation, SASL negotiation or server dialback is not considered to be an XML stanza.

To connect to a server, a client MUST initiate an XML stream by sending an opening <stream> tag, optionally preceded by a text declaration specifying the XML version and character encoding. The server SHOULD then reply with a second XML stream back to the client. Once the client has completed SASL negotiation, it may send an unbounded number of XML stanzas over the stream to any recipient on the network. To close the stream, the client sends the closing </stream> tag, after which both sides SHOULD terminate the underlying connection.

The stream attributes are to, from, id, version and xml:lang. The to attribute should be used only in the header from the initiating entity and must name a hostname serviced by the receiving entity. The id attribute is created by the receiving entity as a session key for the initiating entity's streams, must be unique within the receiving application, and must be both unpredictable and nonrepeating because it may be security-critical.
sections.plainLanguage: A connection carries two streams, one in each direction, and each stream stays open for the life of the connection. The stanzas are written into them one after another. Before any stanza is sent, the two sides use the stream to agree on security and on which device is talking.

sections.title: XML Stanzas
sections.content:
After TLS negotiation if desired, SASL negotiation and resource binding if necessary, XML stanzas can be sent over the streams. Three kinds of stanza are defined for the jabber:client and jabber:server namespaces: <message/>, <presence/> and <iq/>. Five attributes are common to all three: to, which specifies the JID of the intended recipient; from, which specifies the JID of the sender; id, which a sending entity may use for its own internal tracking; type, which gives detailed information about the purpose of the stanza, where the only value common to all three stanza kinds is error; and xml:lang, which gives the default language of any human-readable character data in the stanza.

The message stanza can be seen as a push mechanism, in which one entity pushes information to another, similar to the communications that occur in a system such as email. All message stanzas SHOULD possess a to attribute naming the intended recipient, and a server receiving such a stanza SHOULD route or deliver it to that recipient.

The presence element can be seen as a broadcast or publish-subscribe mechanism, in which multiple entities receive information about an entity to which they have subscribed. A publishing entity should send a presence stanza with no to attribute, and the server should broadcast or multiplex it to all subscribing entities, though it may also send presence with a to attribute to be routed to one recipient.

Info/Query, or IQ, is a request-response mechanism, similar in some ways to HTTP. The data content of the request and the response is defined by the namespace declaration of a direct child element of the IQ element, and the interaction is tracked by the requesting entity through the id attribute. The id and type attributes are REQUIRED for IQ stanzas, and the type must be one of get, for a request for information or requirements, set, which provides required data, sets new values or replaces existing values, result, the response to a successful get or set, and error, which reports a problem with a previously sent get or set. An entity receiving a get or set MUST reply with an IQ of type result or error, preserving the id of the request, and an entity receiving a result or error MUST NOT respond with a further IQ response.

Stanza errors are recoverable, unlike stream errors, and so an error stanza includes hints about what the original sender can do to remedy the error. The entity that detects an error MUST return a stanza of the same kind with a type of error, the stanza MUST contain an <error/> child element, and an entity that receives an error stanza MUST NOT respond with a further error stanza, which helps prevent looping.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of packet travel on the stream. A message is a one-way push, like email. Presence is broadcast to whoever is subscribed. An IQ is a question that must be answered, and the id attribute ties the answer to the question. Errors come back as a stanza of the same kind with the type set to error.

sections.title: TLS, SASL and Resource Binding
sections.content:
When negotiating XML streams in XMPP 1.0, TLS SHOULD be used and SASL MUST be used. The initial stream and the response stream MUST be secured separately, although security in both directions MAY be established through mechanisms that provide mutual authentication. An entity SHOULD NOT attempt to send stanzas before the stream has been authenticated, and if it does, the other entity MUST NOT accept those stanzas and SHOULD return a <not-authorized/> stream error and then terminate both the XML stream and the underlying TCP connection. That rule applies to stanzas only, not to the elements used for stream negotiation.

XMPP includes a method for authenticating a stream by means of an XMPP-specific profile of the Simple Authentication and Security Layer protocol. SASL provides a generalized method for adding authentication support to connection-based protocols, and XMPP uses a generic XML namespace profile for SASL. If the receiving entity is capable of SASL negotiation, it MUST advertise one or more authentication mechanisms in a <mechanisms/> element in reply to the opening stream tag, provided that tag included a version attribute of at least "1.0". Any XML character data within the elements used during SASL negotiation MUST be encoded using base64, and no whitespace characters may be sent within the root stream element as separators between elements, which helps ensure byte precision for the security layer.

After SASL negotiation, the initiating entity may want or need to bind a specific resource to the stream. In general this applies only to clients: to conform to the addressing format and the stanza delivery rules, there MUST be a resource identifier associated with the client's node@domain, so that the address used over that stream is a full JID of the form node@domain/resource. The client sends a new stream header after SASL succeeds, and the server replies with a stream header and a list of available stream features. If the server requires the client to bind a resource, it MUST include an empty <bind/> element in that list. The client then binds a resource by sending an IQ stanza of type "set" containing data qualified by the XMPP binding namespace. It may ask the server to generate the resource identifier by sending an empty <bind/> element, or specify one itself as the character data of a <resource/> child. The server MUST be able to generate a resource identifier on a client's behalf, and one it generates MUST be unique for that node@domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Before any stanzas flow, the two ends protect the channel with TLS and then prove who they are with SASL. After that the client picks or is given a resource name, which completes its address so that a reply can be routed to one particular device or session rather than to the account in general.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The term high security refers to the use of security technologies that provide both mutual authentication and integrity checking. When using certificate-based authentication, a chain of trust SHOULD be established out of band, although a shared certificate authority signing certificates could allow a previously unknown certificate to establish trust in band. Implementations MUST support high security and service provisioning SHOULD use it, subject to local security policies.

When an XMPP peer communicates with another peer securely, it MUST validate the peer's certificate. There are three cases: the peer holds an end entity certificate certified by a chain terminating in a trust anchor; the peer certificate is certified by a certificate authority not known to the validating peer; or the peer certificate is self-signed. In the first case, the validating peer must either verify the certificate according to the rules of X.509 and then check it against the expected identity of the peer, in which case a subjectAltName extension of type "xmpp" must be used as the identity if present, or show the certificate to a user for approval including the entire chain, cache it, and in future connections verify that the same certificate was presented and notify the user if it has changed. In the other two cases, implementations SHOULD act as in the second option.

A compliant client implementation MUST support both TLS and SASL for connections to a server, and a compliant server implementation MUST support both for inter-domain communications. For historical reasons a compliant implementation SHOULD also support Server Dialback. Client-to-server communications MUST NOT proceed until the DNS hostname asserted by the server has been resolved, and such resolutions should first attempt to resolve the hostname using an SRV service of "xmpp-client" and protocol of "tcp", with a fallback to ordinary address record resolution using the "xmpp-client" port of 5222. The IP address and method of access of clients MUST NOT be made public by a server, nor are any connections other than the original server connection required, which helps protect the client's server from direct attack or identification by third parties. Inter-domain connections likewise MUST NOT proceed until the asserted DNS hostnames have been resolved, and it is OPTIONAL for any given domain to communicate with other domains at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends must check each other's certificate, and the RFC is strict about how: either check it against the name the peer claims, or ask a person to approve it once and then notice if it changes later. A server must also not reveal a client's IP address to anyone else, and a domain may simply refuse to talk to other domains if its operator prefers.

messages.label: OPEN XML STREAM
messages.note: The client opens a stream to its own server.

messages.label: RESPONSE STREAM
messages.note: The server opens the stream back.

messages.label: STANZA
messages.note: After TLS, SASL and binding, stanzas flow over the stream.

messages.label: SERVER-TO-SERVER STREAM
messages.note: The server routes the stanza to the domain that owns the address, opening a stream if needed.

THE FOUR TYPES OF AN IQ STANZA

items.label: GET
items.desc: A request for information or requirements.

items.label: SET
items.desc: Provides required data, sets new values or replaces existing values.

items.label: RESULT
items.desc: The response to a successful get or set.

items.label: ERROR
items.desc: Something went wrong with a previously sent get or set.
